publicSurface.javaNullAdaptation: TimeSpan and CancellationToken are value types natively but nullable Java carriers. Freeze Java-only null guards separately: timeout null or invalid timeout before token null for the two-argument overload; token-null rejection before internal fast paths. Do not label Java-null cases native observations.

sourceSemantics: Task.cs 5779-5787 casts TimeSpan.TotalMilliseconds to long (truncate toward zero), validates -1 through 4294967294 inclusive, then casts to uint. Validation happens before completed/cancellation fast paths. Fractional values in (-2,-1) truncate to -1; (-1,1) truncate to zero; upper bound plus a submillisecond fraction can truncate to the maximum. Use exact tick inputs around boundaries.

Task.cs 2832-2849 priority: completed source OR infinite/no-cancel => original identity; otherwise already requested caller token => new FromCanceled; otherwise zero => faulted new TimeoutException task; otherwise new pending promise.

CancellationPromise attaches to source first, then finite timer, then UnsafeRegister; constructor checks completion again and cleans up late-published resources (2862-2912). Source completion may occur between initial fast-path check and attachment; attachment on an already completed source invokes synchronously.

The first successful terminal transition wins. Source canceled copies source CancellationToken and original cancellation dispatch info; source fault copies original fault objects; source success supplies success (2917-2930). Caller cancellation creates cancellation with caller token; timeout creates a TimeoutException. Other contenders are no-ops.

Cleanup order is registration.Dispose, timer.Dispose, source.RemoveContinuation (2934-2938). TrySet completes and dispatches continuations before Cleanup; do not assert resource cleanup must already be finished merely because Status is terminal or a first inline user continuation is blocked.

Runtime completion actions are distinct from user await callbacks: Task.cs 3442-3613 queues second-and-later await callbacks first, then executes first await callback and eligible runtime actions in their original list order. Runtime actions do not consume the first-await slot. An async source (including canceled Delay) queues arbitrary-code completion actions. Late runtime attachment invokes directly (4528-4531); late user OnCompleted queues.

Original source and caller CTS remain borrowed. Timeout/canceling a wrapper never stops, disposes or completes its source, never requests cancellation of caller/source CTS, and never removes another waiter's or user's continuation. Original completion after a losing wait still reaches its own consumers.

privateContract.continuations: Replace the internal Action-only list with a small ordered private entry type carrying either Action or an owned completion action. Give each completion action unique object identity. Add/remove under existing Task lock; invoke outside it. Late add observes fully published payload and invokes immediately outside lock. Removal before detachment removes only its exact entry; removal after detachment may lose to invocation, whose terminal try-complete is idempotent. No producer authority or public hooks added to TaskBridge.
privateContract.dispatch: Preserve existing Action-only paths exactly. With mixed entries, queue all but the first user await callback before the synchronous pass; execute runtime actions and first user callback in original remaining order. Honor the source async-dispatch flag for arbitrary-code actions, without copying that flag to the wait promise. Keep work/state publication outside callback catch scopes. Preserve existing asynchronous failure reporting, rejection fallback and non-inheriting daemon boundaries.
privateContract.waitState: Private per-wait state owns one result Task, borrowed original, one removable source action, optional finite timer handle and optional caller registration. Separate resource monitor from task monitor; cleanupRequested plus publish-or-dispose handles completion-before-publication. Terminal payload uses the existing complete overload and CompletionAttempt winner flag so finally cleanup still runs after a dispatch failure. No resources disposed or user code invoked while either monitor is held.
privateContract.cleanup: Winner detaches/clears owned handles and requests cleanup idempotently; Dispose registration before canceling timer, then remove source action, using finally protection so a Java infrastructure failure cannot skip later owned cleanup. Repeated cleanup disposes no already-owned handle twice; a handle arriving after cleanup is disposed on publication. Active registration disposal can block another thread but self-disposal must not deadlock. Timer cancellation need not suppress a callback already delivered; loser completion remains harmless.
privateContract.constructionFailures: If private timer/registrar scheduling throws, detach the source action and release acquired resources, retaining the primary error and suppressed cleanup errors under an explicitly Java-only contract. Test source completion/cancellation occurring before the failing allocation; do not fabricate a native factory-failure observation for default TimeProvider.System.
privateContract.controls: Use small immutable per-invocation timer/registrar/executor/barrier seams, reusing existing patterns. No mutable global scheduler, generic race framework, reflection-based production access or public System mutation API. Held executors and manually delivered timer callbacks are private Java controls, never claimed as observed native queued scheduling.
